1:
The table itself is explained before the miracle. Lightfoot produces rabbinic evidence that Jewish tables were better spread on the sabbath, and on grounds of piety: one rabbi meets an unexpected guest with cake prepared in honour of the day, another buys of thirteen butchers to be sure of the best. Ellicott adds that such feasts were often luxurious, subject only to the food being cold, the sabbath luxury of the Jews becoming proverbial. Clarke turns this to account: the day was made for body as well as soul, and should not be one of austerity, least of all for the labouring poor. Barnes fences the precedent with conditions — Christ was travelling, went to do good, and used the occasion to reprove vice — beyond which, he says, the example cannot be pleaded for sabbath dinner-parties.

Ellicott renders the phrase for the host as one of the rulers of the Pharisees, and takes him for a Sanhedrist like Nicodemus, or else high in the lay hierarchy Pharisaism had developed. Robertson finds in the watching a periphrastic imperfect middle, watching on the sly and with evil intent, as in Mark 3:2; Clarke reaches the same sense and then loses patience, calling it a baseness one would have thought only devils capable of, to invite a man to table merely for a better chance of accusing him, and setting against it the Persian robber who, tasting salt in a dark treasury, walked out empty-handed. Henry, citing Hammond, adds that it violates every law of hospitality to seek advantage against a guest taken under one's protection.

Whether the sick man was placed there is disputed. Gill says he was brought and set there on purpose; Clarke thinks the Pharisee produced him, not doubting the sight would move Christ; Barnes calls it not improbable; Calvin argues from the circumstances, since a stranger could neither be at the table by accident nor enter a private house without consent — a design as foolish as it was wicked, since they knew what Christ did on such occasions. Wesley denies it: nothing suggests an insidious design, and the man probably came hoping for a cure. Henry notes that neither he nor his friends asked anything: Christ prevented him before he called. Cyril has him standing silent from fear of the Pharisees, so the Lord did not ask whether he would be made whole but healed him at once: where a great good follows we need not care that fools take offence. Ellicott and Robertson note this is the only case of the disease in the Gospels, the word strictly technical, another mark of the physician.

Over the counter-question they divide on the text: Ellicott and Robertson agree the better manuscripts read a son or an ox rather than an ass, Ellicott adding that the familiar pairing would tempt a copyist one way and nothing would tempt him back. Ellicott supplies the casuistry appealed against: food might be let down to a beast in a pit, but no attempt to draw it out till the rest was over — though Lightfoot shows the doctors dispensing freely where an animal was worth money. That is Henry's point too: it is their own ox, worth money, and many dispense for their own interest with what they will not dispense with for God's glory. Calvin keeps to the principle: the law requires only that men rest from their own works, and this is God's. Theophylact presses harder, that a day which does not admit good works is accursed, and Bede that they broke the sabbath by covetousness who charged Christ with breaking it by charity. Gregory finds it fitting he was healed in that company, the bodily infirmity of one expressing the mental disease of the others; Bede, following Augustine, likens him to a covetous rich man, whose thirst grows with the water in him.
7:
Whether this is a parable at all is queried. Barnes says the word means rather a precept, a rule for attending a feast; Ellicott calls it hardly a parable in the modern sense but more than a bare precept, and links it with the germ of the invective of Matthew 23:6; Wesley keeps the name because several parts are not literal. Robertson explains the seats as the first reclining places, the middle of a couch holding three being the place of honour. Gill notes that the meal cannot have been a wedding feast, since they might not marry on the sabbath, but an ordinary sabbath dinner. Theophylact answers the charge that so small a matter is beneath the Word of God: you would not call him a merciful physician who healed the gout but refused a toothache; and the vainglory that set guests contending under the Saviour's eye was no slight passion.

The advice, they notice, was not new. Clarke says our Lord repeats counsel the rabbins gave their own pupils but were too proud to follow, and quotes Akiba: go two or three seats below your due and sit till they say, Go up higher — better that than Come down. Lightfoot has the same maxim from R. Aquila in the name of Simeon Ben Azzai, drawn out of Proverbs 25:7, and beside it the wise man who took the seat next the prince and, asked why, said he was a wise man. Henry appeals to the same passage of Solomon and repeats from Lightfoot the tale of three guests — prince, wise man and humble man — where the king seated the humble man highest and the prince lowest.

Ellicott states the difficulty most sharply, admitting the counsel looks at first like an artificial and calculating humility, and offering three answers: that precepts of social ethics naturally begin from the prudential, as in the Proverbs this form is borrowed from; that the teaching is lowered to the hearers' weakness, with some tinge of grave and solemn irony, since even by their own reckoning they were grasping the shadow; and that a victory over a dominant weakness, won even from a lower motive, strengthens self-control. Calvin refuses the frame: Christ is not speaking of outward and civil modesty, in which the haughtiest often excel, but of what we are inwardly before God, humility being not merely unfeigned abasement but a real annihilation of ourselves. Basil guards the other flank: to rush contentiously after the lowest place is itself a breach of order, and resistance and contradiction are a stronger token of pride than taking the first seat; it belongs to the host to arrange the sitting. Barnes turns it into a defence of manners: religion does not make men rude or pert.

The reversal, patristically read, is no rule of observed life. Cyril says the sentence is spoken according to the divine judgment, not human experience, in which those who chase glory commonly get it and the humble stay obscure; Bede argues the same from the conclusion, since not everyone who exalts himself before men is abased by them, and reads the whole mystically of the marriage feast of the Church, where one bidden earlier must give place to a worthier bidden later, and where then shalt thou have glory is well said, that we may not seek now what is kept for the end. Calvin makes the ground plainer: whoever claims merit must of necessity make war on God. Ellicott hears the saying echoed in 1 Peter 5:5. Ambrose ties the scenes together: the dropsical man cured first, then humility taught at the table. Henry ends where pride is likeliest touched: instead of being proud that so many give place to us, it should humble us that there are so many to whom we must give place.
12:
Theophylact marks the turn: having advised the invited, Christ now advises the inviter against feasting to gain the favour of men. How far the prohibition reaches is then argued. Calvin says those who read it as an absolute condemnation of entertaining kindred take away part of civility, since it would be barbarous to rank relatives with strangers; the point is that customary courtesies are no proof of charity, and that to feast the rich in hope of a return is not generosity but commercial exchange. Barnes reduces it to a supplement: call not only your friends, but also the poor. Clarke condemns what is spent to flatter the rich or procure a return, that money belonging properly to the poor. Wesley leaves the offices of courtesy where they were but finds a higher duty implied, that we be sparing towards those who do not need it, to assist those who do. Bede is careful that friends and kinsmen are not forbidden as though entertaining them were a crime — Christ does not say sin is committed against you, only that such intercourse fails to merit everlasting life.

The host himself is judged more severely. Ellicott sees in that sabbath feast only an ostentatious hospitality calculating on a return in kind: not wrong in itself, but unable to take the place the Pharisee assumed for it among good works, since being repaid on earth excluded it from the reward of the resurrection. Calvin thinks Christ singled him out as too addicted to pomp and too eager for the applause of the rich. Henry puts it in household arithmetic — one feast for the rich will make a great many meals for the poor — and quotes Pliny, that we should give to our poor friends, not to those who do not need us. Robertson notes the two words are breakfast and dinner, the prohibition being of the habit of inviting only such guests.

Chrysostom presses the duty into practice. If a man shrinks from receiving the poor in the best chamber, let him admit Christ below among the servants, or make the poor man his doorkeeper, for where there is alms the devil dares not enter. The humbler the brother, he says, the more Christ comes through him, whereas whoever entertains a great man does it commonly from vainglory or interest. We should be troubled not when a kindness goes unreturned but when it is repaid, since what man does not repay God will. To the objection that the poor are unclean: wash him and seat him at your table, and if his garments are dirty give him clean ones. Origen reads the four classes as conditions of soul — the ignorant to be enriched, the wounded in conscience healed, those wandered from reason set straight, those who discern not the truth brought to the true light.

On the closing promise Ellicott observes this is the first occurrence of the word resurrection in our Lord's teaching, and that in using it he accepts the fundamental doctrine of the Pharisees' own system while rebuking their pride — a precedent for Paul at Acts 23:6. Bede explains the qualification: though all rise, it is called the resurrection of the just because in it they do not doubt they are blessed. Gill lets the blessing be temporal or spiritual, and adds that the poor will themselves pray for such a benefactor. Clarke collects the rabbinic praises of charity — Job set a door in each quarter of his house for the poor, but Abraham was reckoned more charitable, since he travelled the whole land to seek them out. Tertullian turns the passage against Marcion: because the recompense is forbidden now and promised at the resurrection, this is the plan of the Creator, who dislikes those that love gifts and follow after reward, and whose the invited were.
15:
The guest's exclamation is read four ways. Eusebius takes him to identify the resurrection of the just with the kingdom of God, commending the recompense just promised; Cyril calls him carnal and a careless hearer who thought the reward of the saints would be bodily; Augustine answers that he sighed after something far off while the bread he wanted lay before him: who is the Bread of the kingdom but he who called himself the living bread? Open not the mouth but the heart. Barnes explains the mistake historically: the Jews expected a temporal prince, and a reign in which the ancient just would rise to share — a notion the parable corrects. Robertson calls it a pious platitude, of ignorance or hypocrisy, the banquet being a stock rabbinic figure for heavenly bliss which Jesus used himself. Ellicott dissents: it is more natural to hear a burst of honest and unwonted enthusiasm than a hypocritical bid to draw out some condemnable saying. Clarke prefers the reading of many manuscripts, dinner rather than bread, since a dinner was what they sat at.

Robertson keeps the parable distinct from the wedding feast of Matthew; Ellicott calls it the first appearance of the feast imagery in our Lord's teaching, the giver being God and the bidden primarily the Jews. The second summons is documented: Barnes cites Thomson that a sheikh still sends a servant at the hour with the very words, come, for the supper is ready; Robertson cites Tristram that among the Arab tribes refusing it amounts to a declaration of war. Gill offers John the Baptist, Christ, or the apostles for the servant; Ellicott, the whole order of prophets and apostles. Cyril reads him as Christ, who emptied himself and took a servant's form, sent at supper time because the Word took our nature in the last age and not the first.

The excuses are attacked first on their own terms. Lightfoot observes how unmannerly they are if evening was coming on, no hour to inspect newly bought ground or try oxen; Robertson presses the same, that the land would not move and the oxen would not run away. Wesley arranges them as a descent — one pleads his own will, the next a pretended necessity, the third impossibility — all perishing by things in themselves lawful. Ellicott finds the sting in the law: Moses allowed a new marriage, house or vineyard to excuse a man from military service, and these guests treat the invitation as though it were a conscription. Then the allegory. Augustine makes the five yoke the five senses, paired in eyes, ears and nostrils and doubled in the mouth and in the pleasure of touch, called oxen because through them earthly things are ploughed for by men who believe nothing but what they see; and the man goes not to feed them but to prove them, so curiosity rather than delight is condemned. Gregory adds that the senses know only what lies without, and that the two who beg to be excused mix a humble word with a proud act. Ambrose sees three classes shut out — Gentiles, Jews and heretics — the five yoke being the ten commandments on their two tables, and is careful that marriage is not blamed, only purity held in greater honour.

Gregory sets the two delights against each other — bodily pleasures longed for till they are had and loathed after, spiritual pleasures loathed till they are had and then the more desired — which is why mercy recalls the despised feast to memory; and the sentence following is terrible, so that none should slight the call, lest when he wishes to enter he cannot. Henry turns it on the hearers: hearts full of the world, laying house to house and field to field, have ears deaf to the invitation, and each might have deferred his errand a day.
21:
Ellicott observes that the indignation is stronger in the parallel parable, where apathy passes into scornful outrage, and distinguishes the two words for the places searched: the piazza of an Eastern town, and the lane hardly wide enough to ride through. In application these are the by-ways of Jewish life, the courts no scribe would enter, and the four classes are the publicans and harlots who pressed into the kingdom — the adjectives repeated exactly from the earlier precept, so that in his own feast our Lord follows the rule he had just laid down for feasts on earth. Barnes reads the sequence nationally, the first bidden being Jews at ease and those in the streets Gentiles. Gill and Wesley take the servant's report as a picture of ministers rendering account of their hearers, often with grief.

On the room that remains Barnes lets himself go: millions have been saved and heaven is not yet full, harps other hands may strike and seats others may occupy; and he sets against it the message we might have had to carry, that every place is filled. Ellicott makes the point exegetically: space-limits cannot be introduced into the interpretation at all, the many mansions having room for all who come. Clarke keeps to the custom: when guests are too numerous for the host's court, a larger is borrowed.

The word rendered compel is where the commentators part company, and sharply. Clarke argues from usage that it means to prevail on by earnest entreaty, the same verb serving when Christ constrained his disciples into the vessel, where nothing but persuasion can be meant; and he ends flatly that no other constraint is ever recommended in the Gospel, every other compulsion being antichristian, submitted to only by cowards and knaves, and productive of hypocrites. Ellicott calls it painfully true that men have read into the words a sanction for force and penalties, and answers that such means may make proselytes and hypocrites but not converts, the only apostolic instances of that compulsion being Saul forcing men to blaspheme and the Judaisers forcing circumcision. Robertson quotes Vincent to the same effect, that the constraint is against the reluctance such poor creatures would feel; Wesley allows only the violence of love and the force of God's word. Against them stand Augustine, who answers those pleading that they will enter of their own will that a will is what necessity applied from without gives rise to, and Calvin, who, having described the master raking together the offscourings of the world rather than admit the ungrateful, adds that he does not disapprove Augustine's use of the passage against the Donatists, faith being voluntary and yet such methods useful for subduing the obstinate.

The hedges are given a social reading. Lightfoot asks who those among the hedges are and finds them in the potters of 1 Chronicles 4:23, whom the Vulgate places among plantations and hedges and whom Solomon and Kimchi describe as making pots, planting and building mud walls; he thinks the Targumist on that verse extravagant. Barnes describes the hedge from Hackett as a thorn fence, often prickly pear as thick as a man's body, and its labourers as the poorest class — while cautioning that parts of a parable are put in for keeping and should not be forced, the great point being the calling of the Gentiles. Ellicott sees rather the tramps and squatters sleeping under a fence, in application the wanderers of the outlying Gentile world. On the closing exclusion all three moderate it: Barnes says it cannot mean no Jew would be saved, but none who so decidedly rejected the offer; Ellicott, that a parable deals roughly with general facts and passes over what would answer to the remnant according to the election of grace; Robertson, that we need not say Jesus shuts the door against Jews who may yet turn to him.
25:
The turn in the road is read as deliberate. Robertson calls it a dramatic act, a check thrown across the enthusiasm of crowds who followed simply to be following; Theophylact says many followed lukewarmly, so Christ showed what kind of man a disciple must be; Gill explains their expectation, the nation being big with carnal notions of a temporal kingdom. Henry sees a mixed multitude like that which left Egypt — many for love and more for company — and infers that ministers must always separate the precious from the vile. Gregory states the principle behind the harshness: the mind kindles at heavenly rewards and would already be there, but great rewards are not reached except by great labours.

What hate means occupies most of them. Barnes says flatly that it is to love less, since we are not at liberty literally to hate our parents, the fifth commandment forbidding it, and points to the idiom of Jacob and Esau and of Leah. Clarke argues the same way from Matthew's loveth more than me. Robertson resists the softening: the verb is strong, and though the language is one of exaggerated contrast it must not be watered down till the point is gone; it bites where choice enters, when a parent stands against Christ. Ellicott notes that the form is harder than in Matthew, not hating having replaced loving more, and is addressed not to the Twelve but to the whole crowd of would-be followers: he asks nothing less than the heart, and it cannot be given by halves. Wesley reads it comparatively, yet so that a man actually renounces field, oxen and wife and acts as if he hated them when they stand in competition. Gregory meets the objection that we are elsewhere told to love enemies: we may love those bound to us by flesh and still refuse to know them as they stand in the way of God, a man being loved by being hated when his carnal advice is not heard. Ambrose asks why anyone should be preferred before his Lord, who said, Who is my mother?

The clause about a man's own life is handled more carefully. Gregory takes it as proof that the hatred springs from love and not passion, since we rightly hate our own soul when we refuse its desires and wrestle with its pleasures — what contempt brings to a better condition being loved by hatred. Cyril will not let this become a general renunciation: Paul kept his life that he might preach Christ, and counted it not dear only when it had to be spent to finish his course. Robertson puts the same balance in modern terms: martyrdom an ever-present possibility, neither courted nor shunned, love for Christ taking precedence even over the instinct of self-preservation — and in naming the wife Christ has answered the third excuse of the parable just told. Henry keeps it practical: those who decline Christ's service for fear of disobliging a relative or losing a customer give cause to suspect where their love lies.

On the cross Chrysostom insists that no beam of wood is meant but death kept always before the eyes, as Paul died daily. Basil hears in it the announcement of the Lord's death, which baptism anticipates when the old man is crucified. Gregory divides the bearing in two, the affliction of the body by abstinence and the making of a neighbour's necessities our own, and explains that and come after me is added because some are abstinent for vainglory. Robertson notes that the verb for bearing is used of the cross nowhere else in the New Testament but here and of Christ in John 19:17, crucifixion having been common in Palestine since Antiochus Epiphanes. Ellicott adds the timing: after what the disciples heard between Peter's confession and the Transfiguration, the figure was growing daily more terrible.
28:
What sort of tower is meant is disputed. Barnes takes it for a place of defence or observation, high enough to see an enemy coming and strong enough not to be easily taken; Clarke thinks it no more than a dwelling house with battlements, used for air, refuge and prayer; Robertson allows either, or a tower-shaped building raised for ornament. He is better on the verb, which comes from the pebble used in voting, as our calculate is from a pebble too, and on the noun for cost, from a root meaning to devour. Basil allegorises the watch-tower into the understanding, given us to preserve the good and mark the enemy's approach; Gregory draws the plain rule, that everything we do should be preceded by anxious consideration. Gill makes the tower the profession itself, which must rest not on descent or education or bare knowledge but on Christ.

Calvin explains why the warning was needed: men yield to slight temptations because they had pictured an unmixed enjoyment, as if always in the shade and at their ease, and no one is fit to serve Christ till he has undergone a long preparation for warfare. Building is tedious and war threatens destruction, yet men spend on both without hesitation — while a far better reward waits on those who build God's temple. He guards it twice: it would be idle to press a parable in every point, so the suit for peace must not become a compromise with our spiritual enemy; and the meditation must not discourage us, since the materials and the arms come from heaven. Henry itemises the cost — mortified lusts, self-denial, perhaps reputation, estate, liberty, life — and asks what that is beside what it cost Christ to purchase what comes to us without money and without price. Theophylact warns against laying a foundation and not ending the work, like the disciples who went back, for then a man is laughed at by men and by devils.

Ellicott suspects a side-glance at the war the Tetrarch's divorce drew him into against Aretas, his first wife's father, where his army was destroyed and Josephus saw the beginning of all his later misfortunes. Spiritually he pairs the tower with the house built on rock, and finds in the campaign both the Christian's conflict and the greater war Christ had entered, whose counted cost was his life. Theophylact makes the enemy sin reigning in the mortal body, the devils its satellites, outnumbering us because spiritual against corporeal; Cyril widens the muster to fleshly lust and the law of sin raging in the members; Augustine reduces the odds to the simplicity of the Christian against the subtlety of the devil.

The embassy divides them. Augustine finds it a second reproach, since those who have forsaken all may still be unable to bear the threat of a coming temptation and make peace by consenting to sin. Gregory takes it as counsel: at that trial we are two against one, the enemy sifting us in thought as well as deed, and while the judge is still afar off we should send tears, works of mercy and the propitiatory victim as our embassy. Ellicott makes it a lesson in thoroughness: if we will not pay for the war, better come to terms; the worst folly is a wavering will and an impossible neutrality. Augustine ties both parables to the conclusion: the cost of the tower and the strength of the ten thousand mean only that a man forsake all he has, in which the hating of father and mother is contained. Ellicott prefers renounce, the word afterwards used at baptism; and Bede distinguishes renouncing from leaving, since few are perfect enough to leave all, but every believer must so hold the world as not to be held by it.
34:
Bede begins from the substance: salt is water and air with a slight mixture of earth, and dries the fluent nature of corrupt bodies so as to keep them from decay — which makes the comparison fit, since the disciples are regenerated by water and the Spirit and, living spiritually, change the corrupt life of men around them. Theophylact widens the application from the gifted teacher to the private man; Wesley says the same in four words, every Christian and more eminently every minister. Barnes keeps to the plain use, that salt preserves and keeps from putrefaction.

Lightfoot supplies the connection, which he thinks a very good one: Christ had just been teaching that a man must weigh beforehand what he undertakes, lest having begun he faint and go back — apostatise, and become unsavoury salt. He adds a Hebrew observation, that the word for savourless carries also the sense of foolish, the same term serving in can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt and in the verse rendered nor charged God foolishly. Bede puts the difficulty as a question: if a man once enlightened falls back, having cast away the sweetness he tasted, alarmed by troubles or allured by the world, what other teacher is left to correct him? Ellicott hears in the question itself an almost hopeless sadness. He takes the salt for the purifying element in life, the principle of unselfish devotion, whose aspect here is self-renunciation, so that as the renunciation is incomplete the savour goes; and he asks what other purifying influence remains when the love of Christ has failed.

The double uselessness is worked out carefully. Barnes corrects the rendering — not fit for the land but not fit as land, since nothing can be sown on it — and adds that it will not serve as manure either. Gill enters a mild demurral, that salt does make land fruitful if not too much is used, though he cites Pliny on the other side. Ellicott makes the most of the difference from the parallel sayings, which he thinks proves this one independent: a humbler use of salt is in view, mingled with the dunghill to prepare ground for seed. A corrupt church cannot exercise an influence for good even on the secular life of the nation it represents; the man whose religion has become hypocrisy cannot even be a good citizen, or help others forward by teaching or example. Both are fit only to be cast out and become a by-word. Bede says the same of the individual, who can then neither bear fruit himself nor instruct others, and must be separated from the unity of the Church. Robertson notes only that the word for dunghill is late vernacular and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.

The closing formula is taken as deliberate. Theophylact explains it by the manner of the discourse, which had been in parables and dark sayings, so that our Lord rouses his hearers not to take the salt indifferently: let a man understand as far as he has wisdom, the ears standing for the mind's perceptive power. Bede adds the condition, that he hear not by despising but by doing what he has learnt. Ellicott finds in the repetition of the words that closed the earlier parable a mark of our Lord's sense of how deep his meaning went; Robertson observes that both this and the salt saying are among those Christ repeated. Barnes draws the application back to the profession of religion: a man who sustains to true piety the relation this insipid mass bears to good salt is useless in the church, and will be rejected.
